nodes.title: HashiCorp Vault tokens: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Tokens are the core authentication mechanism in Vault — every authenticated client uses a token to make API calls. Vault token types, TTLs, and policies determine what a client can do.

flashcards.front: Root token — when and why to use it?
flashcards.back: Generated during 'vault operator init'; has unlimited access. Should be revoked immediately after bootstrapping policies — never used for day-to-day operations.
Service token: stored in Vault, supports renewal, can create child tokens. Batch token: lightweight, encrypted, not stored — cheaper for high-throughput use cases but cannot be renewed or looked up.
TTL: how long until the token expires unless renewed. Max TTL: the absolute ceiling a token's lifetime can be extended to — renewal cannot push past it.
Creates a token without a parent; revocation of the creator's token does not cascade to this token. Useful for long-lived service accounts.

nodes.title: Where does the cluster store its state?

choices: etcd
kube-proxy
CoreDNS
kubelet

nodes.explanation: etcd is the consistent, distributed key-value store that holds all cluster state. Only the kube-apiserver talks to it directly — every other component reads and writes state through the API server.

nodes.title: Role-based access control: Key Ideas
nodes.content: RBAC assigns permissions to roles, then users to roles — a layer of indirection that scales. Azure's RBAC, AWS's IAM, Kubernetes RBAC, and GCP's IAM all share the same mental model. Mastering one transfers directly to the others.

flashcards.front: Why use roles instead of granting permissions to users directly?
flashcards.back: Roles separate WHO from WHAT. Add a person to a role, they inherit the permissions. Remove them, they lose access instantly. Auditing: 'who can read prod?' becomes 'who's in the prod-readers role?' instead of scanning thousands of user-level policies. Onboarding/offboarding becomes role membership changes, not 500 permission grants.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between a built-in role and a custom role?
flashcards.back: Built-in: cloud-provided, covers common patterns (Owner, Contributor, Reader, Storage Admin). Can't be modified. Custom: you define the exact actions allowed — pick when built-ins are too broad or too narrow. Cost of custom roles: maintenance — every new service adds actions you may need to add.

flashcards.front: Scope — why is it as important as the role?
flashcards.back: Same role at different scopes = wildly different power. 'Contributor' at the subscription scope = god mode on the whole subscription. 'Contributor' on one resource group = limited to that group's resources. Always scope at the smallest unit that's practical — never grant subscription-level if resource-group-level works.

flashcards.front: RBAC vs ABAC — when do you need attributes?
flashcards.back: RBAC: permissions tied to fixed roles. Works great until you need rules like 'engineers can read their own team's resources but not others'. ABAC (attribute-based) evaluates request attributes (user.team, resource.team) at runtime. Most clouds support both — start with RBAC, add ABAC tags when the role explosion becomes painful.

questions.q: You need to grant a ServiceAccount named 'deploy-bot' in the 'ci' namespace read-only access to Deployments across all namespaces. What combination of resources should you create?
choices: A ClusterRole with get/list/watch on deployments, and a RoleBinding in the 'ci' namespace
A Role and RoleBinding in the 'ci' namespace
A Role with get/list/watch on deployments in every namespace, and a ClusterRoleBinding
A ClusterRole with get/list/watch on deployments,.
questions.explanation: To grant cluster-wide access, you need a ClusterRole (defines permissions at cluster scope) and a ClusterRoleBinding (binds the subject across all namespaces). A RoleBinding—even referencing a ClusterRole—only grants access within the binding's namespace. Roles themselves are namespace-scoped and cannot grant cluster-wide access. and a ClusterRoleBinding referencing the ServiceAccount

questions.q: A developer reports that `kubectl get pods` returns `Error from server (Forbidden)`. Their kubeconfig context points to the right cluster and `kubectl config view` looks clean. What is the most likely root cause?
choices: The kubelet on the developer's laptop is not running
The user or ServiceAccount has no Role/ClusterRole binding for `get pods`
The developer needs to run `kubectl auth login` to refresh their tokens
The kube-apiserver TLS certificate has expired on the control plane; TLS expiry does not affect which pods appear forbidden
questions.explanation: A 403 Forbidden means the request reached the API server but the RBAC authoriser denied it — the calling subject has no Role or ClusterRole binding granting the `get` verb on `pods`. An expired API server cert would surface as a TLS handshake error, not Forbidden. There is no `kubectl auth login` subcommand. The kubelet is irrelevant on a client machine.

questions.q: You need to verify what actions a ServiceAccount 'reporter' in namespace 'monitoring' can perform. Which kubectl command checks if it can list pods in that namespace?
choices: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:monitoring:reporte
kubectl describe serviceaccount reporter -n monitoring
kubectl auth check --user=reporter --verb=list --resource=pods -n monitoring
kubectl get rolebindings -n monitoring | grep reporter
questions.explanation: 'kubectl auth can-i' with --as impersonates the given subject and returns yes/no. The ServiceAccount must be specified in the format system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>. 'kubectl get rolebindings' would require manual parsing and wouldn't show effective permissions from ClusterRoleBindings. 'kubectl describe serviceaccount' only shows metadata.

questions.q: You need to quickly test whether a newly created ClusterRole 'deployment-viewer' provides the correct permissions. A user 'alice' should be able to 'get' and 'list' Deployments cluster-wide. Which sequence of commands validates this?
choices: kubectl get clusterrole deployment-viewer -o yaml && kubectl get clusterrolebinding | grep alice; inspecting the clusterrole YAML shows rules but not whether alice can actually list deployments
kubectl describe clusterrolebinding alice-binding
kubectl auth reconcile --as=alice -f role.yaml
kubectl auth can-i get deployments --as=alice && kubectl auth can-i list deployments --as=alice
questions.explanation: 'kubectl auth can-i' with --as impersonates the user and tests a specific permission. Running it for both 'get' and 'list' on deployments validates the effective permissions without needing to inspect YAML manually. This tests the complete RBAC chain (ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding). 'kubectl get clusterrole -o yaml' only shows what the role defines, not whether alice has it bound. 'kubectl auth reconcile' applies RBAC manifests, not tests permissions.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: You need a ClusterIP Service for an application but want to define your own cluster IP address (e.g., 10.96.100.50). Which Service spec field allows this?
choices: spec.clusterIP: '10.96.100.50'
spec.internalIP: '10.96.100.50' - spec.internalIP is not a valid field for setting a custom clusterip
spec.loadBalancerIP: '10.96.100.50'
spec.externalIPs: ['10.96.100.50']
questions.explanation: spec.clusterIP allows you to set a specific IP address for a ClusterIP Service, provided the address is within the configured service CIDR and is not already in use. spec.externalIPs exposes the service on additional IPs outside the cluster. spec.loadBalancerIP is for cloud LoadBalancer Services. spec.internalIP is not a valid Service field.

questions.q: A NodePort Service is created for a web application. A developer cannot reach the app at <NodeIP>:30080 from outside the cluster. The pod is Running and `kubectl get endpoints` lists the Service endpoint. What should you check next?
choices: The Service's clusterIP allocation in the cluster CIDR
The pod's readinessProbe configuration and timing
Whether kube-proxy is in IPVS rather than iptables mode
Whether the node firewall or cloud SG allows inbound on the
questions.explanation: Pod Running + endpoint listed means kube-proxy has installed the iptables/IPVS rule and traffic that reaches the node will be forwarded. The next-most-common blocker is the host firewall or cloud security group dropping inbound traffic on the NodePort (default range 30000-32767) — that must be explicitly allowed.

questions.q: You need to expose a Service externally using a cloud provider's load balancer. Which Service type should you use?
choices: ExternalName
NodePort
ClusterIP with an ExternalName
LoadBalancer
questions.explanation: Service type LoadBalancer provisions an external cloud load balancer (on supported providers like AWS, GCP, Azure) and assigns it an external IP. NodePort exposes the service on each node's IP at a static port but requires you to manage your own external load balancer. ExternalName creates a CNAME alias to an external DNS name. ClusterIP is internal-only.

questions.q: You need a Service that maps requests for 'legacy.internal' to an external hostname 'legacy.example.com' without proxying traffic. Which Service type achieves this?
choices: ExternalName with spec.externalName: legacy.example.com
ClusterIP with an endpoints object pointing to the external IP
LoadBalancer with an annotation pointing to legacy.example.com
Headless Service with a manual DNS CNAME record
questions.explanation: An ExternalName Service creates a CNAME DNS entry in CoreDNS. When pods query the service name, they receive a CNAME pointing to spec.externalName. No proxying or IP allocation occurs. This is useful for abstracting external services. A manual Endpoints object would require knowing the external IP, not DNS name. Headless services return pod IPs, not CNAMEs.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: You need to take a snapshot backup of etcd running as a static pod. The data directory is /var/lib/etcd and certificates live in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/. Which command correctly creates a snapshot the API server can use for a future restore?
choices: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=.../ca.crt
etcdctl backup --data-dir /var/lib/etcd --backup-dir /backup/etcd.db --endpoints https://127.0.0.1:2379 --tls
etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd --skip-tls-verify --endpoints 127.0.0.1:2379
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-master -- etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --tls
questions.explanation: `etcdctl snapshot save` is the v3 API command, and it must authenticate to the live cluster — that means passing --endpoints, --cacert, --cert, and --key. `etcdctl backup` is the deprecated v2 syntax. `--data-dir` is not a flag for `snapshot save`. Running through `kubectl exec` without mounting the certs still fails because the binary inside the pod can't read host certs without --cacert/--cert/--key.

questions.q: After restoring an etcd snapshot to a new data directory /var/lib/etcd-restore, what must change so the etcd static pod starts using the restored data?
choices: Run `kubeadm etcd restore /var/lib/etcd-restore` to register the new directory
Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
Delete the etcd pod and let the kubelet automatically pick the restored directory
Run `systemctl restart etcd` on the control-plane node after symlinking the path
questions.explanation: etcd runs as a static pod under /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. Both the --data-dir flag passed to the etcd container AND the hostPath volume that backs that directory must point at /var/lib/etcd-restore. The kubelet detects the manifest change on disk and restarts the pod. `kubeadm etcd restore` does not exist; pod deletion alone is not enough because the kubelet recreates the pod from the unchanged manifest; etcd is not a systemd service when run as a static pod.

questions.q: A static pod manifest placed in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ is not starting. The pod does not appear in 'kubectl get pods -A'. What should you check first?
choices: Confirm the pod is listed in 'kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending'
Verify the pod has a valid ServiceAccount token mounted
Check the kube-scheduler logs for scheduling errors; the manifest placed in /etc/kubernetes/manifests is not consulted by the scheduler
Check the kubelet logs on the node where the manifest was placed.
questions.explanation: Static pods are managed entirely by the kubelet, not by the API server scheduler. If a static pod isn't starting, the kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) will show parsing errors, file permission issues, or image pull problems. The kube-scheduler is not involved in static pod lifecycle. Static pods may briefly not appear in kubectl if the kubelet hasn't registered the mirror pod yet. using 'journalctl -u kubelet'

questions.q: The kube-scheduler pod is not running after a cluster upgrade. It is defined as a static pod. Where would you find its manifest to investigate?
choices: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
/var/lib/kubelet/config/kube-scheduler.yaml
/opt/kubernetes/scheduler/kube-scheduler.yaml
/etc/systemd/system/kube-scheduler.service
questions.explanation: In a kubeadm-provisioned cluster, all control plane components (kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, etcd) run as static pods. Their manifests are in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ on the control plane node. The kubelet watches this directory and manages the pods. A misconfiguration in the YAML (e.g., wrong image tag, invalid flag) would prevent the scheduler from starting.

questions.q: A Deployment named 'web-app' has 5 replicas but only 3 pods are running. 'kubectl describe deployment web-app' shows the ReplicaSet has 5 desired but 3 available. What is the most likely next diagnostic step?
choices: Scale the deployment down to 3 replicas to match the current state
Delete and recreate the Deployment with the same spec
Check 'kubectl get pods' for the deployment's pods and look for
Run 'kubectl rollout restart deployment/web-app' immediately; restarting pods directly does not explain why fewer pods are running
questions.explanation: When a Deployment's desired replica count exceeds available, the pods themselves hold the diagnostic information. 'kubectl get pods' filtered to the deployment's selector reveals pod states (Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, etc.), and 'kubectl describe pod' shows events with specific error messages like image pull failures, resource constraints, or node affinity issues. then 'kubectl describe pod <pod-name>' for events

questions.q: A Deployment rolling update is stuck. `kubectl rollout status deployment/api` hangs with `1 old replicas are pending termination`. Which command best helps you find which pod is blocking the rollout?
choices: `kubectl delete replicaset <old-rs-name>` and let the deployment recover; deleting the replicaset bypasses termination hooks and loses diagnostic data
`kubectl get replicasets -l app=api` to compare desired and ready counts
`kubectl rollout pause deployment/api` to freeze the in-flight rollout
`kubectl describe pod <old-pod>` to inspect termination events and hooks
questions.explanation: A stuck rollout pending termination usually means a pod is ignoring SIGTERM, a preStop hook is hanging, or `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is set high. Describing the old pod surfaces the relevant events (`Stopping container`, hook execution). Listing replicasets shows replica counts but not why a pod won't go away. Deleting the old RS or pausing the rollout sidesteps diagnosis.

questions.q: A NetworkPolicy is applied to pods labeled 'app=api'. After applying the policy, the API pods can no longer reach the database pods labeled 'app=db' on port 5432. The policy spec has an empty 'egress: []' array. Why?
choices: NetworkPolicies only apply to ingress traffic by default; ingress-only policies leave egress empty and unrestricted by default
An empty 'egress
The policy must be in the same namespace as the database pods to allow traffic
NetworkPolicies do not apply to TCP traffic on port 5432 without explicit protocol specification
questions.explanation: In Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, if 'policyTypes' includes 'Egress' and the 'egress' array is empty, all egress traffic from the selected pods is denied. An empty array means 'no rules match', which results in a default deny. To allow egress to the database, you must add an egress rule specifying the db pod selector and port 5432.

questions.q: After applying a new NetworkPolicy, pods in namespace `app` can no longer reach the kube-dns Service (10.96.0.10:53). What must be added so DNS works again?
choices: An egress rule on the policy allowing UDP/TCP 53 to the kube-system namespace
A podSelector that matches the kube-dns pods inside the same policy object; a podSelector alone inside the same policy namespace does not restore DNS egress
A namespaceSelector allowing all ingress from kube-system on the policy
An ingress rule allowing the kube-dns Service to reach the app pods on 53
questions.explanation: Once a NetworkPolicy with `policyTypes: Egress` selects a pod, ALL outbound traffic is blocked unless explicitly allowed. DNS queries go to port 53 on CoreDNS in kube-system, so the fix is an egress rule allowing UDP and TCP 53 to that namespace (or to the CoreDNS pods specifically). Ingress rules don't affect outbound DNS lookups.
